demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Vignette: Maya, Age 33

Maya has been a paramedic for nine years. She is the kind of person her colleagues describe as steady - the one who stays calm when everyone else is falling apart, the one who knows what to do before anyone has finished explaining the situation. She married her husband, Daniel, four years ago, and until eighteen months ago, she would have said her life felt full in the ways that mattered.

Eighteen months ago, Maya was driving an ambulance to a non-emergency transfer call. It was mid-afternoon, the kind of ordinary shift that doesn't require much thought. She moved through an intersection on a green light, and a cyclist - a teenage boy, sixteen years old - came from the left, invisible until he wasn't. She did not see him in time. The impact was immediate and catastrophic. The boy sustained a traumatic brain injury and spent six weeks in intensive care. He survived, but he walks with a permanent limp and has significant cognitive difficulties. Maya knows this because she looked him up. She wishes she hadn't.

She was cleared of wrongdoing. The investigation concluded the boy had run a red light. Her colleagues told her it wasn't her fault. Her supervisor told her it wasn't her fault. A counsellor the service provided told her the same thing. None of it has reached the part of Maya that matters.

In the weeks after the accident, she returned to work because she thought movement would help. It didn't. She began to notice that she couldn't drive the ambulance without her hands going cold and rigid on the wheel. She started taking longer routes to avoid that intersection, then longer routes to avoid intersections with bike lanes, then longer routes still. Her partner on shift noticed but said nothing for a long time. When he finally asked, she told him she was fine.

She is not fine. At night, she replays the moment of impact with a precision that feels almost mechanical - the sound, the lurch of the vehicle, the way she sat in the driver's seat for several seconds before she could make herself move. She wakes at two or three in the morning and lies still beside Daniel, certain that something terrible is about to happen, though she cannot name what. When she does sleep, she dreams of the boy's bicycle, crumpled under the wheel, and she wakes up with her heart already racing.

At work, she functions, but only barely. She has become hypervigilant in a way that exhausts her - scanning every intersection, every pedestrian, every cyclist on the periphery of her vision. She startles badly when her radio crackles unexpectedly. She has stopped eating lunch in the common room because her colleagues' easy conversation about difficult calls makes her feel something between rage and shame that she can't explain to herself. She used to be the one who debriefed the newer staff. Now she avoids them.

At home, she is quieter than she used to be. Daniel tries. He asks how she is and she says tired, because that is true and because it is easier than the rest of it. She has stopped going to the Saturday morning market they used to visit together because there are always cyclists there, and the sight of them - unhelmeted, casual, alive - makes her chest tighten in a way she cannot manage in public. She knows, intellectually, that this is not reasonable. Knowing does not help.

What Maya carries, and has not yet found words for, is this: she believes that the accident revealed something true about her. That despite nine years of saving people, of doing everything right, she is the kind of person who can destroy a life in an ordinary afternoon. The boy's face, which she only glimpsed for a moment, has become more familiar to her than almost anything else in her world.
